o:
We walk a spiral path: north, west, south, east, repeating, with step lengths given by `distance`. We must decide whether any two segments of the path intersect (including touching at endpoints, as in Example 3 where the path returns to the origin). Because the direction always rotates counter-clockwise by 90 degrees, the path is a spiral that either keeps expanding outward or starts shrinking; a crossing can only happen shortly after the spiral begins to turn inward. This structure means we do not need general segment intersection over all pairs — only a constant number of local conditions involving the last few segments.

**Example 1** `[2,1,1,2]`: north 2 to (0,2), west 1 to (-1,2), south 1 to (-1,1), east 2 to (1,1). The last eastward segment passes through x=0 at y=1, which lies on the first northward segment — crossing. **Example 2** `[1,2,3,4]`: the spiral expands outward every turn, so no crossing is possible. **Example 3** `[1,1,1,2,1]`: after going around once, the fifth move (north 1) lands exactly on the origin, where the path started — touching counts as crossing.

With n up to 10^5, an $O(n^2)$ pairwise check is borderline but risky; the intended solution is $O(n)$ using case analysis on consecutive segments.
k: The counter-clockwise spiral either grows forever (no crossing) or turns inward, and crossings only occur within a few segments after it starts shrinking.
All self-crossings reduce to exactly three local patterns involving at most the last six distances.
Touching at a point (including returning to the start) counts as crossing.

a.i: Build the list of segment endpoints as we simulate the walk, then for each new segment test intersection against every earlier non-adjacent segment using the standard orientation-based segment intersection test (two segments intersect iff orientations straddle each other, handling collinear on-segment cases). Since touching counts as crossing, collinear overlap must be detected too.
s: Simulate moves, recording points p0..pn; directions cycle N, W, S, E.
For each new segment (p[i-1], p[i]), compare against segments (p[j-1], p[j]) for j <= i-2.
Use orientation tests: segments AB and CD intersect if orient(A,B,C)*orient(A,B,D) <= 0 and orient(C,D,A)*orient(C,D,B) <= 0, plus collinear on-segment checks.
Return true on the first intersection; otherwise false.
a.t: O(n^2) — each of the n segments is tested against up to n earlier segments.

a.i: Because directions rotate counter-clockwise, the path is a spiral. If it never shrinks relative to two steps back, it spirals outward forever and cannot cross. A crossing can only occur when the spiral turns inward, and then it must match one of exactly three patterns: (1) current leg crosses the leg from four steps ago (`d[i] >= d[i-2]` and `d[i-1] <= d[i-3]`); (2) current leg touches the endpoint of the leg four steps back when lengths coincide (`d[i] == d[i-2]` and `d[i-1] + d[i-3] >= d[i-4]`); (3) current leg crosses the line of the leg five steps back when the spiral has just started shrinking (`d[i-2] >= d[i-4]`, `d[i-3] <= d[i-1]`, `d[i-1] + d[i-5] >= d[i-3]`, and `d[i] + d[i-4] >= d[i-2]`). Checking these three conditions per index gives a linear scan.
s: For each i >= 3, check case 1: d[i] >= d[i-2] && d[i-1] <= d[i-3] -> true.
For each i >= 4, check case 2: d[i-1] == d[i-3] && d[i] + d[i-4] >= d[i-2] -> true.
If no condition fires, return false.
a.t: O(n) — a single pass with O(1) work per element.
a.sp: O(1) — only indices into the input array are used.

w: In an interview, mention the brute-force orientation test briefly to show geometric fluency, then derive the O(n) case analysis — it is what interviewers expect for this problem. Common pitfalls: forgetting that touching (Example 3, returning to the origin) counts as crossing; missing case 2 (equal-length legs causing an endpoint touch) and case 3 (crossing just after the spiral starts shrinking); and integer overflow when summing two distances up to 10^5 in Java/C++ (use 64-bit or note 2*10^5 fits in int). Edge cases: arrays shorter than 4 can never cross. Likely follow-ups: how would you handle clockwise rotation (mirror the same cases), or arbitrary turn angles (then you truly need general segment intersection, e.g., a sweep line in O(n log n)).
